title: Air Plan Approval; AK; Fairbanks PM2.5 Boundary Redesignation and Clean Data Determination
content: ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION AGENCY 40 CFR Parts 52 and 81 [EPA-R10-OAR-2026-8551; FRL-13545-01-R10] Air Plan Approval; AK; Fairbanks PM 2.5 Boundary Redesignation and Clean Data Determination AGENCY: The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). ACTION: Proposed rule. SUMMARY: The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is proposing to approve a request from Alaska to revise the boundary designation of the existing Fairbanks North Star Borough nonattainment area for the 2006 primary 24-hour fine particulate matter (PM 2.5 ) National Ambient Air Quality Standard (NAAQS). The EPA is proposing to split the existing nonattainment area into two distinct nonattainment areas, an area covering Fairbanks and the Goldstream Valley, and an area covering North Pole. The proposed new areas cover the same geographic area as the existing area. The EPA is also proposing to issue a clean data determination (CDD), for the proposed Fairbanks and Goldstream Valley area (“proposed Fairbanks nonattainment area”) based on a determination that the area is attaining the 2006 PM 2.5 NAAQS. If the EPA finalizes this CDD, certain Clean Air Act (CAA) requirements that apply to the proposed Fairbanks nonattainment area will be suspended for so long as the area continues to meet the 2006 24-hour PM 2.5 NAAQS. The EPA is taking this action pursuant to Clean Air Act sections 107, 110, 172, and 189. DATES: Comments must be received on or before December 16, 2026. ADDRESSES: Submit your comments, identified by Docket ID No. EPA-R10-OAR-2026-8551, at https://www.regulations.gov. Follow the online instructions for submitting comments. Once submitted, comments cannot be edited or removed from Regulations.gov. The EPA may publish any comment received to its public docket. Do not electronically submit any information you consider to be Confidential Business Information (CBI) or other information the disclosure of which is restricted by statute. Multimedia submissions (audio, video, etc.) must be accompanied by a written comment. The written comment is considered the official comment and should include discussion of all points you wish to make. The EPA will generally not consider comments or comment contents located outside of the primary submission ( i.e., on the web, cloud, or other file sharing system). For additional submission methods, the full EPA public comment policy, information about CBI or multimedia submissions, and general guidance on making effective comments, please visit https://www.epa.gov/dockets/commenting-epa-dockets. FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT: Matthew Jentgen, EPA Region 10, 1200 Sixth Avenue, Suite 155, Seattle, WA 98101; by telephone at (206) 553-0340, or by email at jentgen.matthew@epa.gov. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Throughout this document, the use of “we,” “us,” or “our” is intended to refer to the EPA. We use multiple abbreviations and terms in this proposed rule. While this list may not be exhaustive, for ease of reading and for reference purposes, the EPA defines the following terms and acronyms here: Alaska DEC Alaska Department of Environmental Conservation AQS Air Quality System CAA Clean Air Act CDD Clean Data Determination EPA U.S. Environmental Protection Agency NAAQS National Ambient Air Quality Standards PM 2.5 Fine Particulate Matter SIP State Implementation Plan SLAMS State and Local Air Monitoring Station TSD Technical Support Document Table of Contents I. Executive Summary A. What action is the EPA taking? B. What is the legal authority and what are the requirements? II. Background III. Summary of Alaska's Redesignation Request IV. Proposed Action A. Revisions to the Existing Fairbanks Nonattainment Area Boundary B. Clean Data Determination for the Proposed Fairbanks Nonattainment Area C. Summary V. Transportation Conformity Implementation VI. Statutory and Executive Order Reviews I. Executive Summary A. What action is the EPA taking? The EPA is proposing to approve a request from Alaska to revise the boundary designation of the Fairbanks North Star Borough nonattainment area for the 2006 primary 24-hour PM 2.5 NAAQS. 1 The Agency is proposing to split the existing nonattainment area into two distinct nonattainment areas, a Fairbanks and Goldstream Valley area (“Fairbanks nonattainment area”) and a North Pole area (“North Pole nonattainment area'), that cover the same geographic area as the existing nonattainment area. The EPA is also proposing to issue a CDD for the proposed Fairbanks nonattainment area for the 2006 24-hour PM 2.5 NAAQS. 1 See 40 CFR 81.302. B. What is the legal authority and what are the requirements? The EPA is proposing to revise the existing nonattainment area boundary pursuant to CAA section 107. CAA section 107(d)(3)(D) authorizes the Governor of any State to submit to the Administrator a revised designation of any area or portion thereof within the State. The Agency must approve or deny such proposed redesignation within 18 months. Under CAA section 107(d)(1)(A), any area that does not meet (or that contributes to ambient air quality in a nearby area that does not meet) the NAAQS must be designated as a nonattainment area. The EPA is proposing the CDD pursuant to CAA sections 172 and 189 and 40 Code of Federal Register (CFR) 51.1015 for the proposed Fairbanks nonattainment area. These statutory and regulatory provisions authorize the Agency to suspend certain nonattainment planning obligations if a PM 2.5 nonattainment area has attained the PM 2.5 NAAQS. If finalized, the CDD would relieve the State from the requirements to submit an attainment demonstration, reasonable further progress plan, quantitative milestones and quantitative milestone reports, and contingency measures until the proposed Fairbanks nonattainment area is redesignated to attainment, after which such requirements are permanently discharged; or the EPA determines that the area has re-violated the PM 2.5 NAAQS, at which time the State shall submit such attainment plan elements for the Serious nonattainment area by a future date to be determined by the Agency and announced through publication in the Federal Register at the time the EPA determines the area is violating the PM 2.5 NAAQS. 2 2 40 CFR 51.1015(b). II. Background Under CAA section 109, the EPA has established primary and secondary NAAQS for certain air pollutants (referred to as “criteria pollutants”) and conducts periodic reviews of the NAAQS to determine whether they should be revised or whether new NAAQS should be established. The primary NAAQS represent ambient air quality standards which the Agency has determined are necessary to protect the public health with an adequate margin of safety. The secondary NAAQS represent ambient air quality standards which the EPA has determined are requisite to protect the public welfare from any known or anticipated adverse effects associated with the presence of such air pollutant in the ambient air. PM 2.5 is one such NAAQS. Following promulgation of a new or revised NAAQS, the EPA is required by CAA section 107(d)(1) to designate areas throughout the United States as attainment, nonattainment, or unclassifiable for the NAAQS. Effective December 18, 2006, the EPA revised the primary and secondary 24-hour PM 2.5 NAAQS to 35 µg/m 3 . 3 3 71 FR 61224 (Oct. 17, 2006). On November 13, 2009, the EPA designated a portion of the Fairbanks North Star Borough as nonattainment for the 2006 24-hour PM 2.5 NAAQS (hereafter referred to as the “existing Fairbanks nonattainment area”) upon evaluation of monitored air quality data for 2006-2008. 4 Based on the 43 μg/m 3 2006-2008 design value at the State Office Building monitoring site, 5 the Alaska Department of Environmental Conservation (Alaska DEC) and the EPA determined that a portion of the Fairbanks North Star Borough was violating the NAAQS or contained sources contributing to a violation of the NAAQS. Alaska DEC noted that exceedances of the standard occur during cold and stagnant weather patterns in the winter season and in the summer months as the result of wildfires which Alaska DEC flagged as “exceptional events” in accordance with the EPA's Exceptional Events Rule at 40 CFR 50.14. 4 74 FR 58688 (Nov. 13, 2009). 5 Located at 675 7th Avenue, Fairbanks, within the proposed Fairbanks nonattainment area. The ambient air monitoring network has continued to evolve since initial designation, with a focus on monitoring areas of expected maximum PM 2.5 concentrations throughout the existing Fairbanks nonattainment area. 6 In November of 2009, Alaska DEC established a multipollutant monitoring station at 907 Terminal Street in downtown Fairbanks, Alaska. This station eventually became the Fairbanks National Core multipollutant monitoring station (NCore), with an Air Quality System (AQS) site identification of 02-090-0034. 7 6 For a map of the locations of air quality monitors in Fairbanks, see Figure 2 of the EPA's Technical Support Document in the docket for this action. 7 Letter from Debra Suzuki, Acting Manager, State and Tribal Program Unit, EPA Region 10, to Barbara Trost, Air and Water Quality Division, Alaska DEC, EPA approval of Alaska DEC's 2010 Air Monitoring Network Plan, Oct. 13, 2010. On March 1, 2012, Alaska DEC established a special purpose monitor near the North Pole Fire Station on Hurst Road (AQS ID: 02-090-0035). 8 Originally, this monitoring station only operated during the winter. However, measured PM 2.5 concentrations from this station indicated it was located in the area of maximum PM 2.5 concentration in the nonattainment area. 9 Therefore, on January 1, 2015, the EPA and Alaska DEC converted this monitor from a special purpose monitor to a state or local air monitoring station (SLAMS) year-round monitor. SLAMS are required by the Agency network design regulations and are used for comparison to the NAAQS. 10 8 Letter from Debra Suzuki, Manager, Air Planning Unit, EPA Region 10, to Barbara Trost, Air and Water Quality Division, Alaska DEC, EPA approval of Alaska DEC's 2015 Air Monitoring Network Plan, Oct. 28, 2015. 9 Alaska Department of Environmental Conservation Annual Air Quality Monitoring Network Plan, June 2015. 10 40 CFR 58.1. In 2019, Alaska DEC established a new SLAMS PM 2.5 monitoring station to characterize expected maximum concentration in the Fairbanks and Goldstream Valley portion of the nonattainment area at the A Street location 11 (AQS ID: 02-090-0040). 12 11 Located at 397 Hamilton Avenue, Fairbanks, within the proposed Fairbanks nonattainment area. 12 Letter from Debra Suzuki, Manager, Air Planning Unit, EPA Region 10, to Ms. Barbara Trost, Division of Air Quality, Alaska DEC, Approval of Alaska DEC 2019 Annual Monitoring Network Plan, Nov. 21, 2019. Regarding the nonattainment planning requirements, on September 8, 2017, the EPA approved the nonattainment plan for the existing Fairbanks nonattainment area as meeting the Moderate area plan requirements under CAA section 189(a). 13 However, the area failed to attain the NAAQS by the Moderate area attainment date, so the nonattainment area was classified as a Serious nonattainment area on May 10, 2017. 14 13 82 FR 42457 (Sept. 8, 2017). 14 82 FR 21711 (May 10, 2017). Subsequently, on September 2, 2020, the EPA determined that the area failed to attain by the Serious area attainment date and denied the State's Serious area attainment date extension request. 15 As a result, Alaska was required to submit a revised SIP submission to meet both the Serious area attainment plan requirements and the additional requirements set forth in CAA section 189(d) by December 31, 2020. 16 Alaska submitted the revised plan on December 15, 2020 (Fairbanks 189(d) Plan). The Fairbanks 189(d) Plan updated a number of chapters of the narrative portion of the State Air Quality Control Plan, adopted and incorporated by reference into State law at 18 AAC 50.030(a). 15 85 FR 54509 (Sept. 2, 2020). 16 40 CFR 51.1003(c). On September 24, 2021, the EPA approved the 2013 base year emissions inventory and the PM 2.5 precursor demonstration elements of the Fairbanks Serious Plan as meeting the Serious area planning requirements. 17 In the same action, the Agency approved other plan components as SIP strengthening, including: (1) the updated Fairbanks Emergency Episode Plan 18 that the State adopted on November 18, 2020, and submitted on December 15, 2020; and (2) the regulatory control measures included in the SIP submissions on October 25, 2018, and November 28, 2018 (in addition to the December 13, 2019, submission). 19 The EPA did not determine as part of the September 24, 2021, approval whether these SIP strengthening components met specific nonattainment plan requirements, including control strategy requirements in CAA section 189 and 40 CFR 51.1010 or the contingency measure requirements in CAA section 172(c)(9) and 40 CFR 51.1014. 17 86 FR 52997 (Sept. 24, 2021). 18 State Air Quality Control Plan, Vol. II, section III.D.7.12 ( i.e., Alaska's planning chapter related to air quality forecasting and curtailment levels). 19 For a description of the specific control measures addressed across the State's SIP submissions, see 86 FR 52997 (Sept. 24, 2021). On December 5, 2023, the EPA acted on the remaining elements required for a Serious nonattainment area that failed to attain by the Serious area attainment date, approving in part and disapproving in part the Fairbanks Serious Plan and Fairbanks 189(d) Plan. 20 20 88 FR 84626 (Dec. 5, 2023). On December 4, 2024, Alaska made a SIP submission (Fairbanks Revised 189(d) Plan) intended to address the nonattainment requirements that were disapproved as part of the EPA's December 5, 2023, final rule. On November 18, 2025, the EPA fully approved the nonattainment plan for the existing Fairbanks nonattainment area as meeting Serious area requirements under CAA section 189(b) and the requirements for failing to attain as a Serious area under CAA section 189(d). 21 The current applicable attainment date for the existing Fairbanks nonattainment area is December 31, 2027. 21 90 FR 51529 (Nov. 18, 2025). III. Summary of Alaska's Redesignation Request On May 18, 2025, the Governor of Alaska submitted a request and accompanying supporting analysis for the EPA to revise the boundary designation of the existing Fairbanks nonattainment area. 22 Alaska requested, under CAA section 107(d)(3)(D), to revise the boundary for the existing Fairbanks nonattainment area by splitting it into two distinct nonattainment areas: a Fairbanks and Goldstream Valley area and a North Pole area. 23 22 Alaska's submittal can be found in the docket for this action. 23 For a map of the proposed nonattainment areas, see Figure 1 of the accompanying Technical Support Document (TSD). For a map of the air quality control zones, see Figure 8 of the TSD. The TSD is available in the docket for this action. The boundaries of the two areas follow the existing air quality control zone boundaries. In 2016, Alaska DEC established three air quality control zones for the purposes of implementing burn bans: a Goldstream zone located on the northwestern portion of the nonattainment area, a Fairbanks zone principally consisting of downtown Fairbanks and surrounding residential and commercial areas, and a North Pole zone principally consisting of the city of North Pole and surrounding residential areas. 24 The proposed Fairbanks nonattainment area combines the Goldstream zone and Fairbanks zone. The proposed North Pole nonattainment area consists of the North Pole zone. 24 Alaska Administrative Code, 18 AAC 50.025. The regulatory air quality monitors in the proposed Fairbanks nonattainment area demonstrate a decrease of PM 2.5 levels since 2014. The design values at the NCore and A Street monitors in the Fairbanks portion of the nonattainment area are well below the 2006 NAAQS for the 2022-2024 and 2023-2025 monitoring periods (particularly when excluding state-flagged exceedances likely due to summer wildfires). Alaska DEC has also demonstrated that the proposed Fairbanks nonattainment area does not contribute to a violation of the 2006 PM 2.5 NAAQS in the proposed North Pole nonattainment area, based on consideration of air quality data, emissions and emissions-related data, meteorology, geography/topography, and jurisdictional boundaries. The EPA is using the technical information contained in Alaska DEC's May 18, 2026, submittal and the most recent complete, quality-assured, and certified air quality data for the 2023-2025 monitoring period to support this proposed action. IV. Proposed Action The Agency is proposing to take two actions. Under the authority of CAA section 107(d)(3)(D), the Agency is proposing to approve Alaska's requested revisions to the existing Fairbanks nonattainment area boundary designation to create two separate nonattainment areas that together cover the same geographic area as the existing nonattainment area. Second, pursuant to 40 CFR 51.1015, the EPA is proposing to make a CDD for the proposed Fairbanks nonattainment area for the 2006 PM 2.5 NAAQS. A. Revisions to the Existing Fairbanks Nonattainment Area Boundary In determining whether to approve or deny a State's request for a revision to the designation of an area under CAA section 107(d)(3)(D), the EPA considers the same factors when the Agency initiates a revision to a designation of an area on its own motion under CAA section 107(d)(3)(A). These CAA section 107(d)(3)(A) factors include “air quality data, planning and control considerations, or any other air quality related considerations the Administrator deems appropriate.” Using CAA section 107(d)(3)(A) as a framework, the EPA considers five factors when evaluating requests under CAA section 107(d)(3)(D): air quality data, emissions and emissions-related data, meteorology, geography/topography, and jurisdictional boundaries. If the EPA finalizes this action as proposed, the existing Fairbanks nonattainment area would be split into two distinct nonattainment areas that together cover the same geographic area as the existing area. One of the proposed separate areas, to be called the “Fairbanks nonattainment area,” would consist of the Fairbanks and Goldstream zones of the current area. The other proposed separate area, to be called the “North Pole nonattainment area,” would consist of the North Pole zone. All areas would continue to be designated nonattainment and classified as Serious for the 2006 PM 2.5 NAAQS. CAA section 107(d)(1)(A)(i) defines “nonattainment” as “any area that does not meet (or that contributes to ambient air quality in a nearby area that does not meet)” the NAAQS. Therefore, consistent with the statute, the EPA will not redraw the boundaries of nonattainment areas where one portion of the area, though monitoring clean data, contributes to the nonattainment of another portion of the area. 1. Proposed Fairbanks Nonattainment Area for the 2006 PM 2.5 NAAQS Based on a consideration of the information submitted by Alaska and other available information discussed in the EPA's technical support document (TSD) included in the docket for this action, the Agency is proposing to find that the air quality data, emissions and emissions-related data, meteorology, geography/topography, jurisdictional boundaries, other air quality related considerations, as well as planning and control considerations, support the State's request to revise the existing Fairbanks nonattainment area boundary. Alaska's May 18, 2026, submittal requested that the EPA split the Fairbanks nonattainment area for the 2006 PM 2.5 NAAQS and create a distinct nonattainment area for the Fairbanks and Goldstream portion of the existing nonattainment area. 25 In this action, the Agency is proposing to revise the existing nonattainment area boundary and create two separate nonattainment areas, acknowledging the differences in the factors contributing to PM 2.5 levels in the separate areas, and thus providing Alaska DEC with additional flexibility in meeting the CAA's nonattainment area planning and emissions control requirements. This includes the ability to account for differences in air quality in the separate areas in the event that one of the new, separate areas attains the PM 2.5 standards faster than the other. 25 Alaska submitted a request to the EPA to split the nonattainment area on November 20, 2015. In a June 12, 2018, letter, Alaska DEC requested that the EPA hold the November 20, 2015, split request in abeyance. Alaska DEC requested that the 2026 Split Request supersede the 2015 request that was held in abeyance. The EPA proposes in this action that, based on consideration of the five CAA section 107(d)(3)(A) factors, the proposed Fairbanks nonattainment area does not contribute to a violation of the 2006 PM 2.5 NAAQS in the proposed North Pole nonattainment area, and thus it is appropriate that the two areas be considered separate for implementation and planning purposes. An analysis of the five factors and a weight-of-evidence approach supports this conclusion. The air quality data in the proposed Fairbanks nonattainment area indicate that the 2022-2024 and 2023-2025 design values are below the 2006 PM 2.5 NAAQS. 26 An analysis of emissions data, considering meteorological and geographical/topographical factors, support the conclusion that the emissions from this area are not contributing to the violations in the proposed North Pole nonattainment area. A detailed analysis supporting this demonstration may be found in the TSD in the docket for this action. 26 Due to data issues, the A Street monitor representing the area of maximum PM 2.5 concentrations in the proposed Fairbanks nonattainment area did not have a valid design value until 2024. The other air quality monitor in the proposed nonattainment area, the NCore monitor, has been below the 24-hour PM 2.5 NAAQS since 2015. Because this action also proposes to find that the proposed Fairbanks nonattainment area is attaining the 2006 PM 2.5 NAAQS, it is not necessary to consider whether the proposed North Pole nonattainment area contributes to a violation of the 2006 PM 2.5 NAAQS in the proposed Fairbanks nonattainment area, as no such violation exists. 2. Proposed North Pole Nonattainment Area for the 2006 PM 2.5 NAAQS The Agency is proposing to approve Alaska's request to create a distinct nonattainment area for the North Pole portion of the current nonattainment area based on air quality data, emissions and emissions-related data, meteorology, geography/topography, jurisdictional boundaries, other air quality related considerations, as well as planning and control considerations. The air quality data in the proposed North Pole nonattainment area remains above the 2006 PM 2.5 NAAQS. However, the proposed North Pole nonattainment area does not contribute to a violation of the 2006 PM 2.5 NAAQS in the proposed Fairbanks nonattainment area. Likewise, based on consideration of the five CAA section 107(d)(3)(A) factors, the proposed Fairbanks nonattainment area does not contribute to a violation of the 2006 PM 2.5 NAAQS in the proposed North Pole nonattainment area. Thus, it is appropriate that the two areas be considered separate for implementation and planning purposes. An analysis of the five recommended factors and a weight-of-evidence approach supports this conclusion. B. Clean Data Determination for the Proposed Fairbanks Nonattainment Area As determined in accordance with 40 CFR 50.18 and Appendix N to 40 CFR part 50, an area is attaining the 2006 PM 2.5 NAAQS if it meets the 2006 PM 2.5 NAAQS, based on three complete, consecutive calendar years of quality-assured air quality data for all monitoring sites in the area. To attain the 2006 24-hour PM 2.5 NAAQS, the three-year average of the annual 98th percentile of the daily 24-hour average PM 2.5 concentrations (PM 2.5 design values) at each site must not exceed 35 µg/m 3 . 27 The air quality data must be collected and quality-assured in accordance with 40 CFR part 58 and recorded in the EPA's Air Quality System (AQS.) 28 Ambient air quality monitoring data for the three-year period must also meet data completeness requirements. 29 A 24-hour PM 2.5 design value is valid if quarterly data capture rates for all four quarters in each year of the three-year period are at least 75 percent. 30 However, years shall be considered valid, notwithstanding quarters with less than complete data (even quarters with less than 11 creditable samples, but at least one creditable sample must be present for the year), if the resulting annual 98th percentile value or resulting 24-hour NAAQS design value (rounded according to the conventions of section 4.3 of Appendix N) is greater than the level of the standard. Furthermore, where the explicit 75 percent quarterly data capture requirement is not met, the 24-hour PM 2.5 NAAQS design value shall still be considered valid if it passes the maximum quarterly value data substitution test. 31 27 40 CFR 50.13(c); Appendix N to 40 CFR part 50, Section 4.2. 28 Appendix N to 40 CFR part 50, Section 3.0. 29 Id. At Section 4.2. 30 Id. 31 Id. According to the EPA's AQS air quality monitor data in the proposed Fairbanks nonattainment area, the 2023-2025 design value at the A Street monitor is 35 µg/m 3 and the NCore monitor is 34 µg/m 3 . 32 These design values include all air quality data and do not include potential data that could be approved by the EPA for treatment as Exceptional Events (in this case, monitoring data influenced by summer wildfires). The design value from the prior 3-year period, 2022-2024, at the A Street monitor was 26 µg/m 3 and the NCore monitor was 24 µg/m 3 , when removing all monitor data that the State determined were influenced by summer wildland fires. 33 The 2023-2025 design values at the A Street monitor is 25 µg/m 3 and NCore monitor is 24 µg/m 3 , after excluding state-flagged data that is influenced by summer wildfires. Therefore, based on recent year 3-year design values below the 35 µg/m 3 24-hour PM 2.5 NAAQS, the EPA proposes to find that the proposed Fairbanks nonattainment area will have attained the 2006 24-hour PM 2.5 NAAQS, and proposes to issue a CDD based on the most recent air quality data at monitors located in the proposed Fairbanks nonattainment area. This proposed action is consistent with the Agency's clean data requirements for PM 2.5 Serious nonattainment areas established in 40 CFR 51.1015. If finalized, this CDD would relieve the requirements for the State to submit an attainment demonstration, reasonable further progress plan, quantitative milestones and quantitative milestone reports, and contingency measures for the proposed Fairbanks nonattainment area, in accordance with 40 CFR 51.1015(b). 32 See EPA's Air Quality System, Preliminary Design Value Report, for the A Street and NCore monitors, included in the docket for this action. 33 For a detailed account of the monitor data influenced by summer wildfire smoke, see EPA's letter concurring on Exceptional Events for the annual PM 2.5 NAAQS, included in the docket for this action. Letter from Angeles Herrera, EPA Region 10, Air and Radiation Division Director, to Jason Olds, Alaska DEC, Air Quality Division Director, March 19, 2026. C. Summary This action proposes to revise the boundary of an existing PM 2.5 nonattainment area by splitting it into two separate nonattainment areas that together cover the same geographic area as the existing nonattainment area. This action also proposes to make a CDD for the 2006 24-hour PM 2.5 NAAQS based on air quality data for one of those proposed areas—the proposed Fairbanks nonattainment area. If the EPA finalizes the boundary revision for the Fairbanks nonattainment area and finalizes the proposed CDD for that area, then the EPA will suspend requirements to submit certain plan requirements to attain the 2006 24-hour PM 2.5 NAAQS, so long as the area continues to attain the standard. These actions do not impose additional requirements. V. Transportation Conformity Implementation Transportation conformity is required under CAA section 176(c) to ensure that federally funded or approved highway and transit activities are consistent with (“conform to”) the purpose of the SIP. 34 The EPA notes for informational purposes that, if this proposal is finalized, when Alaska submits a PM 2.5 control strategy SIP or maintenance plan that addresses either of the two proposed, separate areas, such a SIP would need to include separate motor vehicle emissions budget(s) that apply to the new geographic boundaries for use in transportation conformity. The EPA intends to work with the State and the Fairbanks metropolitan planning organization to provide additional technical assistance for transportation conformity purposes prior to adequate or approved budgets being available for the proposed new, separate nonattainment area boundaries. The EPA notes that the Agency is providing this information to provide additional background for this rulemaking; the Agency is not proposing changes to the transportation conformity regulation in this rulemaking. 34 40 CFR Parts 51.390 and 93. VI. Statutory and Executive Order Reviews This action proposes to revise the boundary of an existing PM 2.5 nonattainment area by splitting it into two separate nonattainment areas that together cover the same geographic area as the existing nonattainment area. It also proposes to make a CDD for the proposed Fairbanks nonattainment area, which if finalized would suspend the requirement to submit certain attainment plan requirements for the 2006 24-hour PM 2.5 NAAQS. This proposed action does not impose additional requirements. title: Air Plan Partial Approval and Partial Conditional Approval; South Carolina; Minor Source Permit Program Revisions and Control of Oxides of Nitrogen and Source Testing Requirements
content: ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION AGENCY 40 CFR Part 52 [EPA-R04-OAR-2017-0359; EPA-R04-OAR-2024-0241; and EPA-R04-OAR-2025-0017; FRL-13063-02-R4] Air Plan Partial Approval and Partial Conditional Approval; South Carolina; Minor Source Permit Program Revisions and Control of Oxides of Nitrogen and Source Testing Requirements AGENCY: Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). ACTION: Final rule. SUMMARY: The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA or Agency) is approving changes to South Carolina's State Implementation Plan (SIP) which revise the State's source testing requirements and its regulations prescribing minor source permit program requirements, including minor new source review (NSR) requirements, and partially approving and partially conditionally approving regulations prescribing control requirements for certain stationary sources of nitrogen oxides (NO X ) in SIP revisions submitted by the State of South Carolina, through the South Carolina Department of Environmental Services (SC DES), on October 1, 2007; July 18, 2011; June 17, 2013; August 8, 2014; January 20, 2016; July 27, 2016; September 5, 2017; April 24, 2020; February 4, 2022; and July 23, 2025. This action is being finalized pursuant to the Clean Air Act (CAA or Act). DATES: This rule is effective December 16, 2026. ADDRESSES: The EPA has established three dockets for this action under Docket Identification Nos. EPA-R04-OAR-2017-0359; EPA-R04-OAR-2024-0241; and EPA-R04-OAR-2025-0017. All documents in the dockets are listed on the regulations.gov website. Although listed in the indices, some information may not be publicly available, i.e., Confidential Business Information or other information whose disclosure is restricted by statute. Certain other material, such as copyrighted material, is not placed on the internet and will be publicly available only in hard copy form. Publicly available docket materials are available either electronically through https://www.regulations.gov or in hard copy at the Multi-Air Pollutant Coordination Section, Air Planning and Implementation Branch, Air and Radiation Division, U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, Region 4, 61 Forsyth Street SW, Atlanta, Georgia 30303-8960. The EPA requests that, if at all possible, you contact the person listed in the FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT section to schedule your inspection. The Regional Office's official hours of business are Monday through Friday 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., excluding Federal holidays. FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT: Faith Goddard, Multi-Air Pollutant Coordination Section, Air Planning and Implementation Branch, Air and Radiation Division, U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, Region 4, 61 Forsyth Street SW, Atlanta, Georgia 30303-8960. The telephone number is (404) 562-8757. Ms. Goddard can also be reached via electronic mail at goddard.faith@epa.gov. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: The EPA uses multiple acronyms and terms in this action. While this list may not be exhaustive, to ease the reading of this preamble and for reference purposes, the EPA defines the following terms and acronyms here: APA Administrative Procedure Act BACT Best Available Control Technology BEA Bureau of Economic Analysis CAA Clean Air Act CEMS Continuous Emissions Monitoring Systems CFR Code of Federal Regulations CMS Continuous Monitoring Systems CO Carbon Monoxide COMS Continuous Opacity Monitoring Systems CPMS Continuous Parametric Monitoring Systems EPA Environmental Protection Agency FIP Federal Implementation Plan FR Federal Register GDP Gross Domestic Product LMP Limited Maintenance Plans MRR Monitoring, Recordkeeping, and Reporting NAAQS National Ambient Air Quality Standard or Standards NEI National Emissions Inventory NESHAPs National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants NO X Nitrogen Oxides NOD Notice of Drafting NSPS New Source Performance Standards NSR New Source Review OAR Office of Air and Radiation OFR Office of the Federal Register PEMS Predictive Emissions Monitoring Systems PM Particulate Matter PM 2.5 Fine PM PM10 Coarse PM PSD Prevention of Significant Deterioration PTE Potential to Emit RFP Reasonable Further Progress SC DES South Carolina Department of Environmental Services SC DHEC South Carolina Department of Health and Environmental Control SCCC South Carolina Chamber of Commerce SCMA South Carolina Manufacturers Alliance SCMC South Carolina Manufacturers + Commerce SIP State Implementation Plan SO 2 Sulfur Dioxide TPY Tons Per Year VOC Volatile Organic Compound Table of Contents I. Executive Summary A. What action is the EPA taking? B. What is the legal authority and what are the requirements? II. Final Action III. Background A. The EPA's August 17, 2017, and January 21, 2025, Proposed Rules B. The EPA's August 19, 2026, Minor Source Permitting Proposed Rule C. The EPA's August 19, 2026, Source Testing and NO X Control Proposed Rule IV. Responses to Comments A. Comments on the EPA's January 21, 2025, Proposed Rule Relevant to This Final Action B. Comments on the August 19, 2026, Minor Source Permitting Proposed Rule C. Comments on the August 19, 2026, Source Testing and NO X Control Proposed Rule V. Incorporation by Reference VI. Statutory and Executive Order Reviews I. Executive Summary A. What action is the EPA taking? In this action, the EPA is finalizing, entirely or in part, as described below, four proposed rulemakings. The EPA is finalizing three actions, one entirely and two in part, in which the Agency proposed to approve changes to the State's minor source permit program, including minor New Source Review (NSR), and one action in its entirety in which the Agency proposed to approve changes to its source testing requirements and to partially approve or conditionally approve changes to the State's regulations prescribing control requirements for certain stationary sources of nitrogen oxides (NO X ) in the South Carolina SIP. Specifically, in this action, the EPA is finalizing portions of an August 17, 2017, Proposed Rule in which the Agency proposed to approve changes to the State's minor source permitting program, including its minor NSR program, in SIP revisions submitted by SC DES through July 27, 2016. 1 The EPA is also finalizing portions of a January 21, 2025, Proposed Rule in which the Agency proposed to partially approve changes to the State's minor source permitting program in SIP revisions submitted through April 24, 2020. 2 Furthermore, the Agency is finalizing an August 19, 2026, Proposed Rule which proposed to approve additional changes to the State's minor source permitting program (hereinafter “2026 Minor Source Permitting Proposed Rule”) in SIP revisions submitted by SC DES through July 23, 2025. 3 Finally, in this action, the EPA is finalizing an August 19, 2026, Proposed Rule which proposed to approve changes to the State's source testing requirements and partially approve and partially conditionally approve changes to South Carolina's NO X control regulations for certain stationary sources (hereinafter “2026 Source Testing and NO X Control Proposed Rule”) in SIP revisions submitted through February 4, 2022. 4 As noted above, there are three dockets supporting this final action. Docket No. EPA-R04-OAR-2017-0359 contains information specific to the August 17, 2017, Proposed Rule; Docket No. EPA-R04-OAR-2024-0241 contains information specific to the January 21, 2025, and August 19, 2026, Proposed Rule which proposed changes to the State's minor source permitting provisions; 5 and Docket No. EPA-R04-OAR-2025-0017 contains information specific to the August 19, 2026, Proposed Rule which proposed changes to the State's source testing requirements and NO X control regulations. 1 See 82 FR 39083. 2 See 90 FR 6954. 3 See 91 FR 53558. 4 See 91 FR 53573. 5 Docket No. EPA-R04-OAR-2024-0241 also contains information specific to a third August 19, 2026, proposed rule which proposed to approve changes to South Carolina's minor source permitting program provisions involving public participation, on which the EPA is not acting in this action. See 91 FR 53547. B. What is the legal authority and what are the requirements? CAA section 110(a)(2)(C) requires that SIPs include a program to regulate the construction and modification of any stationary source as necessary to assure that the National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) are achieved. CAA section 110(a)(2)(C) is the statutory foundation for the regulatory requirements in the portion of the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) at 40 CFR 51.160-51.164, which apply to all new minor sources and modifications under a State's minor NSR program in accordance with 40 CFR 51.160, which sets forth requirements for “legally enforceable procedures” applicable to minor NSR programs. The implementing regulations at 40 CFR 51.160-51.164 serve primarily as the basis for the EPA's evaluation of minor NSR programs, and States have discretion to define the scope of their minor NSR programs within the bounds of CAA section 110 and 40 CFR 51.160-51.164. Under CAA section 110(k)(3), the EPA has a statutory obligation to approve SIP submittals that meet all applicable CAA requirements. 6 Pursuant to CAA section 110(k)(3), the EPA may approve portions of a SIP submittal if those portions meet all the applicable CAA requirements. 6 See 42 U.S.C. 7410(k)(3). Under CAA section 110(k)(4), the EPA may conditionally approve a SIP revision based on a commitment from a State to adopt specific enforceable measures by a date certain, but not later than one year from the date of approval. If the State fails to meet its commitment within one year of the final conditional approval, the conditional approval will be treated as a disapproval. Additionally, under CAA section 110(l), the EPA cannot approve a SIP revision if it would interfere with any applicable requirement concerning attainment and reasonable further progress (RFP) (as defined by CAA section 171), or any other applicable requirement of the CAA. 7 The EPA evaluates CAA section 110(l) non-interference demonstrations on a case-by-case basis considering the circumstances of each SIP revision. 7 CAA section 110(l) also requires each SIP revision to undergo reasonable notice and public hearing at the state level. II. Final Action In this action, the EPA is approving certain changes to South Carolina Code of Regulations Annotated (S.C. Code Ann. Regs.) Regulation 61-62.1, Section II (hereinafter “Regulation 61-62.1, Section II”), Permit Requirements. Specifically, the EPA is approving changes in SIP revisions submitted by SC DES through July 27, 2016, proposed for approval on August 17, 2017, to the prefatory introductory paragraph to Regulation 61-62.1, Section II and subsections II(A), II(C), II(H), II(J), II(M), II(O), and subsection II(B), except for paragraph II(B)(2), subparagraphs II(B)(2)(b), (f), and (h), paragraph II(B)(3), and paragraphs II(B)(5)-(7). The EPA is approving further changes to subsections II(C) and II(H) in a SIP revision submitted by SC DES on April 24, 2020. The EPA is also approving changes submitted by SC DES through April 24, 2020, proposed for approval on January 21, 2025, to subsection II(K) and paragraph II(B)(2), to subparagraphs II(B)(2)(b) and II(B)(2)(f), and to paragraph II(B)(7). Additionally, the EPA is approving substantive and administrative changes to subparagraph II(B)(2)(h), except for the second and third sentences therein, 8 in SIP revisions submitted by SC DES through April 24, 2020, proposed for approval on August 19, 2026. Additionally, the EPA is finalizing further changes to paragraph II(K)(5) in a July 23, 2025, SIP revision, proposed for approval on August 19, 2026. The EPA is also approving administrative edits submitted on April 24, 2020, and proposed for approval on January 21, 2025, to subsections II(A), II(C), II(H), II(J)-II(M), and II(O), and to subsection II(B), except for II(B)(2)(h), which was addressed in the August 19, 2026, Proposed Rule, and paragraphs II(B)(3) and II(B)(5)-(6). 9 8 The second and third sentences in subparagraph II(B)(2)(h) that the EPA is not incorporating by reference state: “Unless otherwise exempt, sources may be exempted under this section at higher emission levels if there is a demonstration that there are no applicable limits or requirements. These applicable requirements include federally applicable limits or requirements.” 9 As noted above, in this action, the EPA is not finalizing changes involving minor source permitting public participation proposed for approval on August 19, 2026. Specifically, in this action, the EPA is not finalizing changes to Regulation 61-62.1, subsections II(D), II(E), II(F), II(G), II(I), and II(N), submitted by SC DES in SIP revisions through April 24, 2020. This final action approves, in part, April 24, 2020, State-effective versions of subsections II(B), Exemptions from the Requirement to Obtain a Construction Permit, and II(H), Operating Permit Renewal Requests, including the renumbering of paragraph II(B)(2) to subsection II(H) and the renumbering of subparagraphs II(G)(4)(a)-(e) to subparagraphs II(J)(2)(a)-(e). However, because the Agency is not, in this action, finalizing changes to, in part, subsections II(E), II(F), II(G), or II(N), certain provisions remain in the SIP with June 24, 2005, State-effective dates, i.e., paragraph II(B)(1) under II(B), Operating Permit, II(G), Conditional Major Source Permits, except for II(G)(4)(a)-(e), and II(H), Synthetic Minor Plant Permits. Therefore, with this final action, Regulation 61-62.1, Section II in the South Carolina SIP contains two subsections numbered II(B) and two subsections numbered II(H), with the State-effective dates noted above. In this action, the EPA is also approving changes to S.C. Code Ann. Regs. Regulation 61-62.1, section IV (hereinafter “Regulation 61-62.1, Section IV”), Source Tests, in their entirety in a SIP revision submitted by SC DES on April 24, 2020, proposed for approval on August 19, 2026. The EPA is partially approving or conditionally approving changes to S.C. Code Ann. Regs. Regulation 61-62.5, Standard No. 5.2 (hereinafter “Regulation 61-62.5, Standard No. 5.2”), Control of Oxides of Nitrogen (NO X ), in SIP revisions submitted through February 4, 2022, proposed for approval on August 19, 2026. Specifically, the EPA is approving changes to Sections I-III and V-VII, including the reorganization of Sections V-VII. The EPA is also conditionally approving the portions of the SIP revisions consisting of the addition of and, as applicable, changes to Regulation 61-62.5, Standard No. 5.2, Section IV at: paragraphs IV(A)(1) and IV(C)(1); the second prefatory paragraph of subsection IV(D); and subparagraphs IV(A)(1)(a)-(d), IV(A)(2)(a)-(c), IV(B)(2)(a)-(b), IV(C)(1)(a)-(d), IV(C)(3)(c)-(d), and IV(D)(2)(a)-(b). Finally, the EPA is approving the remaining portions of Regulation 61-62.5, Standard No. 5.2, Section IV which are added and revised. III. Background A. The EPA's August 17, 2017, and January 21, 2025, Proposed Rules On October 1, 2007, July 18, 2011, June 17, 2013, August 8, 2014, January 20, 2016, and July 27, 2016, SC DES submitted SIP revisions with changes to the State's minor source permitting program provisions in Regulation 61-62.1, Section II, Permit Requirements, which the Agency proposed to approve on August 17, 2017. On January 21, 2025, the Agency re-proposed approval of certain provisions evaluated in the 2017 Proposed Rule, including those that received adverse comments, and did not reconsider, or seek additional comments on, certain provisions evaluated in the 2017 Proposed Rule that did not receive comments. In the January 21, 2025, Proposed Rule, the EPA also proposed to act on further changes to Regulation 61-62.1, Section II in a subsequent SIP revision submitted by the State on April 24, 2020. This action approves, in part, the following changes to the State's minor source permit program requirements, proposed for approval in the August 17, 2017, Proposed Rule: changes to minor source permitting prefatory language; construction permit applicability, exemptions, and permit application requirements; operating permit renewal requirements; permit conditions; and requirements for transfer of ownership or operation and inspection and entry. This action also approves additional changes to SC DES's minor source permit program requirements proposed for approval in the January 21, 2025, Proposed Rule. The following changes were proposed for approval in the 2025 Proposed Rule and are approved in this action, in part: (1) subsequent changes, i.e., changes submitted after the July 27, 2016, SIP revision, to the State's construction permit application and operating permit renewal requirements, which were proposed for approval in the August 17, 2017, Proposed Rule and which the EPA did not reconsider, or seek additional comments on, in the January 21, 2025, Proposed Rule; (2) changes to construction permit exemptions and permitting exceptions, which were re-proposed for approval altogether in the January 21, 2025, Proposed Rule, along with additional changes submitted after the July 27, 2016 SIP revision, where applicable; and (3) universal administrative changes applicable to Section II in its entirety. 10 The details of South Carolina's submissions, as well as the background and the EPA's approval rationale, are described in the respective 2017 and 2025 Proposed Rules. 10 In the January 21, 2025, Proposed Rule, the EPA proposed to disapprove portions of the State's SIP revisions with changes to Regulation 61-62.1, Section II. Specifically, the EPA proposed to disapprove subparagraph II(B)(2)(h); paragraphs II(B)(3), II(B)(5), and II(B)(6); and subsections II(D), II(E), II(F), II(G), II(I), and II(N), for reasons described therein. In this action, the Agency is not finalizing any portions of the January 21, 2025, partial disapproval and, therefore, is also not finalizing universal administrative changes applicable to those provisions proposed in that 2025 Proposed Rule. The EPA is also not responding to adverse comments addressing those portions of the January 21, 2025, Proposed Rule that the Agency is not finalizing as a part of this action. However, in this action, the EPA is finalizing relevant changes to subparagraph II(B)(2)(h), which were subsequently proposed for approval in the August 19, 2026, Proposed Rule. See 91 FR 53558. On August 19, 2026, in addition to the 2026 Minor Source Permitting and Source Testing and NO X Control Proposed Rules, the EPA published a third Proposed Rule which proposed to approve changes to South Carolina's minor source permitting program provisions involving public participation, including administrative changes applicable to those provisions, contingent on the EPA finalizing a proposed change to relevant national regulations. See 91 FR 53547. In this action, the EPA is not finalizing the changes involving minor source permitting public participation proposed for approval in that August 19, 2026, Proposed Rule. The EPA received one set of adverse comments on the 2017 Proposed Rule in a joint letter from the Sierra Club, the Center for Biological Diversity, and Our Children's Earth Foundation. These comments are available in the docket for the August 17, 2017, Proposed Rule. 11 In this action, the EPA is not finalizing any portions of the August 17, 2017, Proposed Rule that were the subject of the adverse comment received. Those portions that were the subject of the adverse comment were addressed in the January 21, 2025, Proposed Rule, the Minor Source Permitting Proposed Rule, or an August 19, 2026, proposed rule regarding other portions of the State's minor source permitting program, or South Carolina removed them from the EPA's consideration, as communicated in a July 21, 2026, letter. This action only finalizes portions of the August 17, 2017, Proposed Rule that were not discussed in the adverse comment, as described in Section II of this Final Rule. 11 Docket No. EPA-R04-OAR-2017-0359, available at https://www.regulations.gov/docket/EPA-R04-OAR-2017-0359. In response to the January 21, 2025, Proposed Rule, the EPA received five sets of adverse comments from the following commenters: SC DES, the South Carolina Manufacturers Alliance (SCMA), Century Aluminum, the South Carolina Chamber of Commerce (SCCC), and BMW Manufacturing Co. LLC. 12 The EPA also received a comment from the Southern Environmental Law Center, on behalf of the South Carolina Coastal Conservation League, Sierra Club, and the Southern Alliance for Clean Energy, supporting the disapproval elements of its 2025 proposed action. All comments are available in the docket for the January 21, 2025, Proposed Rule. 13 In this action, the EPA is only addressing a subset of the adverse comments, which were procedural in nature and applied to the entire January 21, 2025, Proposed Rule. The EPA summarizes and responds to these procedural comments, regarding a January 28, 2025, Presidential Memorandum, in Section IV of this action. The remainder of the adverse comments received on the January 21, 2025, Proposed Rule relate to provisions upon which the EPA has re-proposed action in the Minor Source Permitting Proposed Rule and an August 19, 2026, proposed rule, or relate to provisions South Carolina removed from the EPA's consideration in a July 21, 2026, letter. Accordingly, this action only finalizes portions of the January 21, 2025, Proposed Rule that were the subject of general procedural adverse comment, as explained in Section II of this Final Rule. 12 The comment from BMW Manufacturing Co., LLC supported comments on the January 21, 2025, Proposed Rule from SC DES, SCMA, and SCCC, “as they object to the EPA's proposed disapproval,” which the EPA is not finalizing in this action, and contained no additional substantive comments. Where relevant SCMA and SCCC comments are addressed in this action, the EPA's responses also cover BMW Manufacturing Co., LLC's supporting comments, as applicable. 13 Docket No. EPA-R04-OAR-2024-0241, available at https://www.regulations.gov/docket/EPA-R04-OAR-2024-0241. B. The EPA's August 19, 2026, Minor Source Permitting Proposed Rule On October 1, 2007, July 18, 2011, August 8, 2014, April 24, 2020, and July 23, 2025, SC DES submitted SIP revisions that included changes to the State's minor source permitting program provisions in Regulation 61-62.1, Section II. This action approves, in part, the following changes to the State's minor source permit program requirements: administrative changes to reflect the restructuring of the South Carolina Department of Health and Environmental Control (DHEC) to the South Carolina Department of Public Health and the SC DES and certain construction permit exemption provisions, proposed for approval in the 2026 Minor Source Permitting Proposed Rule. The details of South Carolina's submissions, as well as the background and the EPA's approval rationale, are described in the 2026 Minor Source Permitting Proposed Rule. 14 14 See 91 FR 53558 (Aug. 19, 2026). In response to the August 19, 2026, Minor Source Permitting Proposed Rule, the EPA received three sets of adverse comments, one from an individual commenter, and two from anonymous commenters. The EPA also received one set of comments from South Carolina Manufacturers and Commerce (SCMC), 15 one set from SC DES, and one set from an individual commenter, 16 supporting the proposed 2026 Minor Source Permitting action. All comments are available in the docket for the 2026 Minor Source Permitting Proposed Rule. 17 The EPA summarizes and responds to the adverse comments on the 2026 Minor Source Permitting Proposed Rule in Section IV of this action. 15 SCMC's comment addressing, in part, the 2026 Minor Source Permitting Proposed Rule was submitted in response to the August 19, 2026, Proposed Rule which proposed to approve certain changes to South Carolina's minor source permitting program provisions involving public participation, which was collocated in Docket No. EPA-R04-OAR-2024-0241 with the Minor Source Public Participation Proposed Rule. See 91 FR 53547. In this action, the EPA is not finalizing the changes involving minor source permitting public participation proposed for approval in that Proposed Rule, but the Agency is addressing the portion of SCMC's comments relevant to the 2026 Minor Source Permitting Proposed Rule, which was collocated in Docket No. EPA-R04-OAR-2024-0241 with the Minor Source Public Participation Proposed Rule. SCMC takes issue with a statement in the August 19, 2026, Minor Source Permitting Proposed Rule which notes that “the current SIP does not include specific exemptions from permitting for sources emitting SO 2, NO X , or CO” and frames the exemptions in the existing SIP inconsistently with the EPA's August 19, 2026, Proposed Rule but “supports [the] EPA's proposed approval of the current exemption thresholds” and “respectfully encourages [the] EPA to finalize,” in part, the 2026 Minor Source Permitting Proposed Rule “as proposed.” See 91 FR 53558, 53564. Therefore, the EPA interprets SCMC's comment as it relates to the 2026 Minor Source Permitting Proposed Rule as wholly supportive and, in this action, is not addressing SCMC's alternate interpretation of the existing SIP exemption. 16 One commenter encourages the EPA to “emphasize oversight, transparency, and protecting air quality.” The commenter also states that although minor sources of air pollution “may produce smaller amounts of pollution individually . . . it is important for the EPA and South Carolina to continue considering how emissions from multiple sources can affect air quality within a community.” The commenter supports the changes proposed to Regulation 61-62.1, Section II in the 2026 Minor Source Permitting Proposed Rule and does not suggest any changes to the EPA's August 19, 2026, Proposed Rule. Therefore, the EPA views this comment as wholly supportive. The commenter also included comments on changes to “changes to South Carolina's minor source permitting . . . public participation requirements” in Regulation 61-62.1, Section II, which the EPA proposed action on in a separate August 19, 2026, Proposed Rule, as previously described in this action. See 91 FR 53547. These comments are outside the scope of this final action. The comment addressing, in part, the August 19, 2026, Proposed Rule which proposed to approve certain changes to South Carolina's minor source permitting program provisions involving public participation was submitted under the 2026 Minor Source Permitting Proposed Rule, which was collocated in Docket No. EPA-R04-OAR-2024-0241 with the Minor Source Public Participation Proposed Rule. See 91 FR 53558. 17 Docket No. EPA-R04-OAR-2024-0241, available at https://www.regulations.gov/docket/EPA-R04-OAR-2024-0241. As noted above, SCMC's comment addressing, in part, the 2026 Minor Source Permitting Proposed Rule was submitted under the August 19, 2026, Proposed Rule which proposed to approve certain changes to South Carolina's minor source permitting program provisions involving public participation. See 91 FR 53547. C. The EPA's August 19, 2026, Source Testing and NO X Control Proposed Rule On October 1, 2007, July 27, 2016, September 5, 2017, April 24, 2020, and February 4, 2022, SC DES submitted SIP revisions including changes to the State's source testing requirements in Regulation 61-62.1, Section IV, Source Tests, and NO X control regulations applicable to certain stationary sources in Regulation 61-62.5, Standard No. 5.2, Control of Oxides of Nitrogen (NO X ). This action approves changes to the State's source testing requirements concerning test plan submission timing and content as well as source testing notification timing and conduct requirements, along with administrative and clarifying edits, submitted by SC DES on April 24, 2020, and proposed for approval in the 2026 Source Testing and NO X Control Proposed Rule. This action also finalizes changes to the State's NO X control regulations submitted by the State on October 1, 2007, July 27, 2016, September 5, 2017, and February 4, 2022, and proposed for approval or conditional approval in the 2026 Source Testing and NO X Control Proposed Rule. Specifically, this action approves a portion of the State's SIP revisions requesting changes to its NO X control regulations under provisions involving applicability and exemptions, definitions, NO X emission limits and/or control requirements for new sources, certain monitoring, recordkeeping, and reporting (MRR) and testing requirements for new sources, and NO X control, notification, and tune-up requirements for existing sources. This action also conditionally approves a portion of the State's SIP revisions requesting changes to certain MRR and testing requirements for new sources in its NO X control regulations. On May 13, 2026, SC DES submitted supplemental materials, including a letter requesting that the EPA conditionally approve portions of the State's NO X control SIP revisions based on a commitment under CAA section 110(k)(4) to adopt and submit corrective revisions to portions of the SIP provisions before the EPA no later than one year after the EPA's conditional approval of South Carolina's submissions. In this action, the EPA is finalizing the partial conditional approval as proposed on August 19, 2026. The details of South Carolina's submissions, as well as the background and the EPA's approval and conditional approval rationale, are described in the 2026 Source Testing and NO X Control Proposed Rule. In response to the August 19, 2026, Source Testing and NO X Control Proposed Rule, the EPA received one set of adverse comments from an individual, and one set from an anonymous commenter. title: Burlington Electric Department; Notice of Application Tendered for Filing With the Commission and Establishing Procedural Schedule for Licensing and Deadline for Submission of Final Amendments
content: DEPARTMENT OF ENERGY Federal Energy Regulatory Commission [Project No. 2756-068] Burlington Electric Department; Notice of Application Tendered for Filing With the Commission and Establishing Procedural Schedule for Licensing and Deadline for Submission of Final Amendments Take notice that the following hydroelectric application has been filed with the Commission and is available for public inspection. a. Type of Application: New Major License. b. Project No.: 2756-068. c. Date Filed: October 30, 2026. d. Applicant: Burlington Electric Department (Burlington). e. Name of Project: Chace Mill Hydroelectric Project. f. Location: The project is located on the Winooski River in the cities of Burlington and Winooski in Chittenden County, Vermont. g. Filed Pursuant to: Federal Power Act, 16 U.S.C. 791(a)-825(r). h. Applicant Contact: James Gibbons, Director of Policy and Planning, Burlington Electric Department, 585 Pine Street, Burlington, VT 05401; telephone at (802) 658-0300; email at jgibbons@burlingtonelectric.com. i. FERC Contact: Joshua Dub, Project Coordinator, Great Lakes Branch, Division of Hydropower Licensing; telephone at (202) 502-8138; email at Joshua.Dub@ferc.gov. j. The application is not ready for environmental analysis at this time. k. Project Description: The project includes an approximately 252.6-foot-long, 29-foot-high dam that includes two spillway sections that are overtopped with inflatable rubber crest gates with maximum crest elevations of 136 feet National Geodetic Vertical Datum of 1929 (NGVD 29) and a powerhouse that includes an intake structure with a trashrack with 0.8-inch clear bar spacing for the upper 8 feet of the trashrack and 2-inch clear bar spacing on the bottom section, and three 2.485-MW Kaplan turbine-generator units, for a total installed capacity of 7.455 MW. The dam creates an impoundment that has a normal surface area of 6.7 acres at 136.0 feet NGVD 29. From the impoundment, water flows through the powerhouse to a 190-foot-long tailrace, where it returns to the Winooski River. Water also flows through the intake structure to a downstream fishway that includes a collection chamber behind the trashracks and a 3-foot-diameter pipe that discharges to the tailrace on the east side of the powerhouse. The project creates an approximately 230-foot-long bypassed reach of the Winooski River. The project includes an upstream fish passage facility that consists of a trap and truck facility with a concrete fish lift located on the west side of the powerhouse. Project recreation facilities include: (1) an approximately 660-foot-long paved walkway on the north shoreline of the impoundment; (2) an approximately 745-foot-long public access trail on the north shoreline of the Winooski River, to the west of the project dam; and (3) a public access and overlook area on top of the powerhouse. The project includes a 200-foot-long access road on the northern bank of the impoundment. Electricity generated at the project is transmitted to the electric grid via an underground 400-foot-long, 13.8-kilovolt transmission line. l. Locations of the Application: A copy of the application may be viewed on the Commission's website at http://www.ferc.gov using the “eLibrary” link. Enter the docket number excluding the last three digits in the docket number field to access the document. For assistance, please contact FERC Online Support at FERCOnlineSupport@ferc.gov, (866) 208-3676 (toll free), or (202) 502-8659 (TTY). A copy is also available for inspection and reproduction at the address in item h above. m. You may also register online at https://ferconline.ferc.gov/eSubscription.aspx to be notified via email of new filings and issuances related to this or other pending projects. For assistance, contact FERC Online Support. n. For public inquiries and assistance with making filings such as interventions, comments, or requests for rehearing, contact the Office of Public Participation at (202) 502-6595 or OPP@ferc.gov. o. Procedural Schedule: The application will be processed according to the following preliminary schedule. Revisions to the schedule will be made as appropriate. Milestone Target date Notice of Acceptance/Notice of Ready for Environmental Analysis May 2027. Filing of recommendations, preliminary terms and conditions, and fishway prescriptions July 2027. p. Final amendments to the application must be filed with the Commission no later than 30 days from the issuance date of the notice of ready for environmental analysis. (Authority: 18 CFR 2.1) Dated: November 10, 2026. Carlos D. Clay, Deputy Secretary. [FR Doc. 2026-23285 Filed 11-13-26; 8:45 am] BILLING CODE 6717-01-P
